outcome: Since 26 January 2024 two things have happened to this bullet. (1) A Caltech-led preprint (Butbaia, Gukov et al.; Zenodo 20 Aug 2026, arXiv 2608.22518) reports new lower-bound records for the maximal determinant at n = 51 and at n ≡ 3 (mod 4) in 103–119; its earliest version used no learning method, and its latest version (1 Oct 2026) describes a reinforcement-learning search, with simulated annealing used for some orders. (2) On 12 Aug 2026 Levent Alpöge announced on X a ±1 matrix of order 668 (encoded as a puzzle), crediting a team of three humans and Claude; if valid it attains Hadamard's bound at n = 668, and secondary reports say the same package covers eleven further multiples of 4 below 2000. Neither event determines the maximal determinant in general.
problem_asks: Parts, enumerated from the statement alone. (1) For each order n ≥ 1, the largest determinant of an n×n matrix whose entries are all 1 or –1, i.e. the function md(n) = max det over {±1}-matrices of order n. Since negating a row changes the sign of det, max det equals max |det|. (2) The bullet asks for the value of md(n) for every n; it names no restricted class of orders and no restricted class of matrices, so no order is excluded. What the statement does not ask, but which the Wikipedia lead uses as context: Hadamard's bound n^(n/2) is attained exactly when a Hadamard matrix of order n exists, which forces n ∈ {1, 2} or 4 | n; and whether Hadamard matrices exist for every multiple of 4 (the Hadamard conjecture, a separate bullet). For n ≡ 0 (mod 4) part (1) is therefore equivalent to asking whether a Hadamard matrix of order n exists; for other n it is a separate question (Ehlich/Barba-type bounds apply and are not attained in general). The 0/1 and complex-entry variants are not parts of this bullet.

events.what_happened: W. P. Orrick, B. Solomon, J. Dowdeswell and W. D. Smith, 'New lower bounds for the maximal determinant problem' (arXiv math/0304410). Per the arXiv abstract as quoted in search snippets (not opened by me): new record determinants for orders 22, 23, 27, 29, 31, 33, 34, 35, 39, 45, 47, 53, 63, 69, 73, 77, 79, 93 and 95, with tabulated values for 67, 75, 83, 87, 91 and 99 per a search summary. The authors conjecture that their n = 22 value is the global maximum for that order. Matrices posted at the authors' maxdet site (indiana.edu/~maxdet).
events.delivers: Explicit ±1 matrices exceeding previously recorded determinants at the listed orders. Lower bounds only; the n = 22 maximality is a conjecture, not a proof, in this paper.
events.remains: Exact md(n) at every listed order (the maximum is not established for these n in this paper) and every other n.
events.directly_checkable: The matrices are published as explicit ±1 arrays; each determinant can be recomputed directly. Not checked by me.
events.direction: Raises lower bounds; does not bear on an upper bound and does not determine any maximum except as conjectured for n = 22.
events.object: Explicit ±1 matrices of the listed orders, with determinants above the earlier records; constructed by computer search and by construction from design-theoretic data. Explicit, not an existence proof.

events.what_happened: Y. Wang et al. (Microsoft Research / UW), 'ThetaEvolve: Test-time Learning on Open Problems' (arXiv 2511.23473; ICML 2026). An open-source framework that runs an LLM with test-time reinforcement learning on open optimisation problems. Its Appendix A.5 uses the 29×29 maximal-determinant task (Hadamard matrices, n = 29) with the score |det H| / (2^28 × 7^12 × 342), and cites Orrick et al. 2003's 2^28 × 7^12 × 320 as the best known. The best ThetaEvolve score in Table 2 is 0.5764 (Distill-Qwen3-8B with RL, step 65); the pure-inference best is 0.5733 and the ProRL-1.5B-v2 RL best is 0.5635. Under the same normalisation the best known scores 320/342 ≈ 0.936 (my calculation).
events.revisions: arXiv v1 28 Nov 2025 (per arXiv page); ICML 2026 publication per search results.
events.delivers: No new determinant for n = 29. A benchmark score of 0.5764 of the normalised target, below the best known. Establishes only that an LLM-based search did not reach the 2003 record at n = 29 in this run.
events.remains: The whole bullet, including n = 29 (the best known 2^28 × 7^12 × 320 is not improved here).
events.directly_checkable: The score is a determinant ratio computed by an evaluator function, per the paper's appendix; not checked by me.
events.doubts: The normalisation uses 342 where the best known uses 320; the paper does not explain the choice in the text I read. Not a result, so no doubt about correctness is needed for the bullet.
events.direction: Does not improve the best known; a negative benchmark result for an LLM-based search at n = 29.

events.what_happened: On 12 Aug 2026 Levent Alpöge (described by QbitAI and Epoch as an Anthropic researcher) posted on X a ±1 matrix of order 668 with HH^T = 668I, encoded in the post and its replies as a puzzle whose decoder is a shell script (per secondary reports). Per QbitAI (13 Aug 2026, Chinese language, quoting the post) the collaborators are Philippe Voinov, Saul Reynolds-Haertle and Claude; QbitAI and Epoch say the same package gives Hadamard matrices for every open order below 2000 without a known instance (QbitAI lists twelve: 668, 716, 892, 1132, 1244, 1388, 1436, 1676, 1772, 1916, 1948, 1964; Epoch says 'all admissible orders up to 2000 where no such instance was previously known'). The X post itself returned HTTP 402 to my fetch, so the primary wording is quoted through a blog post (Nechita) and secondary reports. Epoch's FrontierMath open-problem page lists 'Hadamard Matrix of Order 668' as 'Solved (human + AI)', 'First solved with: Claude (internal Anthropic model)', crediting 'a team of three humans and Claude', with the provisional label dated 12 Aug 2026 in its changelog.
events.revisions: Epoch label 'Solved by AI' provisional from 12 Aug 2026; relabelled 'Solved (human + AI)' on 16 Sep 2026 per Epoch's changelog (as read on the index page).
events.delivers: If the matrix is valid: a Hadamard matrix of order 668 exists, so md(668) = 668^334, Hadamard's bound, attained. That settles n = 668 for this bullet; secondary reports say it settles eleven further multiples of 4 below 2000. It settles nothing for other n, and the general maximal determinant remains open. (For n ≡ 0 mod 4, the maximal determinant equals n^(n/2) exactly when a Hadamard matrix of that order exists, so the existence claim and the bullet's value coincide there.)

events.what_happened: G. Butbaia, J. Tan, P. Vipulanandan, X. Huang, T. Saunders-A'Court, L. Fagan, D. Passaro, M. Tarquini and S. Gukov, 'New Records for the Hadamard Maximal Determinant Problem' (arXiv 2608.22518; a Zenodo copy of v1 is dated 20 Aug 2026, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22024187, with code at github.com/Math-AI-Caltech/hadamard-maxdet). Three arXiv versions. v1 (23 Aug 2026, title 'in Dimensions 51, 107, and 115'): new lower bounds at n = 51, 107, 115 improving previous recorded bounds by 3.1%, 0.44% and 1.68%, with 'the data necessary to construct these matrices'; no learning method. v2 (31 Aug 2026, title 51, 107, 111, 115, 119): adds 111 and 119 with improvements 1.26% and 2.12%; no learning method. v3 (1 Oct 2026, comment 'Updated to include methods'): abstract 'describe[s] several learning-based strategies for reconstruction', compares with simulated annealing as a benchmark, and reports new record determinants 'for orders n≡3 (mod 4) between 103 and 119, as well as n=51'. Method (from the v3 HTML, read through a summarising fetch): the ±1 matrices are built from two m×m circulant matrices A, B with m = (n−1)/2, and the determinant maximisation is recast as a sequence reconstruction from periodic autocorrelation sums; the reconstruction is done by reinforcement-learning policies (a GNN and an autoregressive transformer decoder trained with PPO, GRPO fine-tuning) and by simulated annealing.
events.revisions: Zenodo v1 20 Aug 2026 (n = 51, 107, 115; 3.1%, 0.44%, 1.68%). arXiv v1 23 Aug 2026 (same content). arXiv v2 31 Aug 2026 (n = 51, 107, 111, 115, 119; 3.1%, 0.44%, 1.26%, 1.68%, 2.12%). arXiv v3 1 Oct 2026, 'Updated to include methods' (learning-based strategies; simulated annealing benchmark; orders 103–119 with n ≡ 3 mod 4, plus 51).
events.delivers: Lower bounds (new records over previously recorded values) for the maximal determinant at n = 51 and at n ≡ 3 (mod 4) in 103–119, per the latest version. Ratios to the Orrick (2012) reference, as reported in the v3 appendix: n = 103 ratio 1.0000004; n = 111 ratio 1.0126294; n = 115 ratio 1.0182876; n = 51, all 10 record-breaking PAF-sum targets reconstructed (no ratio given); n = 107 and 119, ratios not given in the part I could read. Optimality is claimed only within the family of circulant-block constructions (the uncorrelated X(A, B), plus a correlated variant in Appendix C), not as a global maximum. Establishes no upper bound and no maximum at any order.
events.remains: The exact maximal determinant at every listed order (51 and 103–119), since only lower bounds are claimed, and every other n. The Hadamard-type upper bounds for n ≡ 3 (mod 4) are not attained by these matrices as far as the paper reports.
events.time_since_posted: about 7 weeks since the first posting (20 Aug 2026), as of 12 Oct 2026
events.directly_checkable: Each matrix is specified by the first rows of two circulant blocks, given in a CSV (n, a, b, normalised determinant D) in the GitHub repository, with a verify.py script and an 'expected verification output' table for n = 51 to 119 (repository README, read through a summarising fetch). These were not run by me. The matrices can be checked by computing det and the claimed ratio.
events.doubts: (a) Scope grew between versions: v1 3 orders, v2 5 orders, v3 adds the learning method and the range 103–119. The v3 title lists 51, 107, 111, 115, 119 but the abstract and body also include n = 103, which the title omits. (b) The learning-based part is credited only for n = 103, 111, 115 (Appendix A.1: 'We exhibit new record–determinant matrices obtained by reinforcement learning in orders…'); for n = 51 the appendix says 'We limited experimentation to simulated annealing in this order', and the 107 and 119 runs are described as simulated annealing on the energy functional. (c) The n = 103 margin is 1.0000004 over the previous record. (d) No referee, no journal, no independent reproduction, and no later paper found in my searches. (e) The author team's background in matrix or design theory was not established by me; Sergei Gukov's public profile in the search results is mathematical physics and reinforcement learning for mathematics. This is neutral context for the judging pass, not a finding against the result.
events.direction: Raises lower bounds at the listed orders; it cuts in favour of the existence of larger determinants than previously recorded at those orders, and does not bear on the conjectured maximum (no upper bound is claimed).
events.object: Explicit ±1 matrices of orders 51 and 103–119 (n ≡ 3 mod 4), each built from two m×m circulant ±1 blocks with m = (n−1)/2 (the uncorrelated X(A, B) construction and, in Appendix C, a correlated variant), specified by the first rows of the blocks, which are determined by PAF-sum targets found by search. Explicit constructions, not existence proofs. The bitstrings are in Appendix A.1 and the CSV (neither read in full by me).

systems.name: reinforcement-learning policy (authors' own; GNN and autoregressive transformer decoder trained with PPO and GRPO fine-tuning; no named model)
systems.what_it_did: Per the v3 appendix, the policies reconstruct the PAF-sum targets into ±1 sequences, and for n = 103, 111, 115 the records were obtained by these policies (Appendix A.1: 'We exhibit new record–determinant matrices obtained by reinforcement learning in orders' — the sentence goes on to name 103, 111 and 115). The Conclusions say: 'we have reformulated the Hadamard maximal determinant problem in orders n≡3 (mod 4) as a reinforcement learning based sequence reconstruction problem'. Against this, the n = 51 records were reconstructed with simulated annealing (Appendix D.1), and the 107 and 119 results are attributed to simulated annealing (Appendix D.2). The learning part is therefore load-bearing for three of the listed orders and not for the others, per the authors' own appendix. No commercial or lab-named model is credited anywhere in the text read.
systems.basis_quote: we have reformulated the Hadamard maximal determinant problem in orders n≡3 (mod 4) as a reinforcement learning based sequence reconstruction problem

ai.disclosed_cost: No money or token figure found. The acknowledgements name compute: Google's TPU Research Cloud (Cloud TPUs), NVIDIA Academic Grant Program GPUs, Nebius Academy cloud, AMD University Program AI & HPC cluster, and the University of Cambridge Computer Lab. Appendix D.2 says the 107 and 119 runs took 'few days'. The paper's acknowledgements also name DARPA cooperative agreement HR0011262E017 as sponsor.

disputes.summary: The Butbaia et al. preprint changes its claimed orders and method between versions. v1 (23 Aug 2026, Zenodo 20 Aug) claims n = 51, 107, 115 with no learning method. v2 (31 Aug) adds 111 and 119. v3 (1 Oct, 'Updated to include methods') adds learning-based reconstruction and states records 'for orders n≡3 (mod 4) between 103 and 119, as well as n=51', while its title still lists 51, 107, 111, 115, 119 and omits 103. The authors' own statements of the scope do not agree.

Attribution of the order-668 result to an AI system is contested or provisional. Epoch's page credits 'a team of three humans and Claude' and says 'First solved with: Claude (internal Anthropic model)', with the label 'Solved (human + AI)' provisional and open to revision if humans contributed significantly to the core ideas. QbitAI says it is unclear whether the result came from an improved search or from a general construction, and that how Claude found the pattern awaits the technical report. The authors' own X post could not be fetched (HTTP 402), so the only authors' words I have are the 'of course claude' and 'a very strong model, a good loopy/agentic harness' lines as quoted in Nechita's blog.

The set of orders claimed for the 668 package is not settled. QbitAI lists twelve orders (668, 716, 892, 1132, 1244, 1388, 1436, 1676, 1772, 1916, 1948, 1964). Epoch says 'all admissible orders up to 2000 where no such instance was previously known'. A 2008 list in a search snippet also includes 1004. I could not reconcile these lists.

Order-668 status sources disagree by date: TheoremDB (snapshot 24 Jul 2026) and the Epoch problem page's earlier text describe the Hadamard matrix of order 668 as unknown; the Epoch changelog and the current Epoch page describe it as solved (human + AI) from 12 Aug 2026. The later Epoch entry is the one I take as current, but it rests on secondary reports.

The date of the Brent–Orrick–Osborn–Zimmermann proof that md(37) = 2^39 × 3^36 is 2009 in one search summary and December 2011 (arXiv 1112.4160, published 2012) by the arXiv ID. I did not open the paper to settle which.

summary: The bullet asks for the largest determinant of a ±1 matrix of each order n, and the Wikipedia lead (opened; its lead says n = 23 is the smallest open case and that the maxima are solved up to n = 22) frames it that way. Before the window the sources show a long run of computer-assisted record and maximum results: Orrick et al. 2003 records and the n = 22 conjecture, Orrick–Solomon 2003 for orders 4k+1, Orrick 2004 for n = 15, Brent–Orrick–Osborn–Zimmermann 2011 for n = 19 and 37 (arXiv ID; the 2009 date in a search summary is unreconciled), Chasiotis–Kounias–Farmakis 2018 for n = 22 (read via OEIS and a survey reference, not opened), and the 2021 survey by Browne et al. with a constant-factor family for n ≡ 3 (mod 4). Within the window, four kinds of event bear on it. (1) Nuñez Ponasso's 2024 dissertation is about complex unimodular matrices; its real-matrix section could not be read. (2) Eliahou's 2025 order-668 matrix is only a 64-modular approximation (Gram matrix ≡ 668I mod 64), so it is not a Hadamard matrix and settles nothing. (3) The 2026 Butbaia et al. preprint on arXiv 2608.22518 (first posted on Zenodo 20 Aug 2026, arXiv v1 23 Aug, v2 31 Aug, v3 1 Oct) gives new lower bounds at n = 51 and n ≡ 3 (mod 4) in 103–119. Its v1 had no learning method. Its v3 adds reinforcement-learning policies and simulated annealing; by its own Appendix A.1, RL produced the records at 103, 111 and 115, and simulated annealing produced the n = 51 targets and the 107 and 119 results. No upper bound and no maximum is claimed; optimality is shown only within a circulant-block family. (4) On 12 Aug 2026 Alpöge announced a ±1 matrix of order 668 with HH^T = 668I, encoded as a puzzle, crediting a team of three humans and Claude; secondary reports say it covers twelve open orders below 2000. Since md(n) = n^(n/2) exactly when a Hadamard matrix of order n exists for 4 | n, a valid matrix would settle md(668), and the other claimed orders, as Hadamard's bound. I could not open the primary post (HTTP 402), any arXiv or repository write-up, or the decoder, so the 668 claim rests on secondary reports, Epoch's provisional 'Solved (human + AI)' label, and a blogger's account of the tweet. The authors' own sentence on Claude's contribution is 'of course claude:))' and 'a very strong model, a good loopy/agentic harness' (as quoted in Nechita's post), which does not say what Claude produced. AI searches on this bullet by name, with AlphaEvolve, GPT, Gemini Deep Think, OpenAI, Lean and formal-conjectures terms, found no AI result on the ±1 maximal determinant apart from the Butbaia et al. learning method and the 668 announcement; ThetaEvolve (Nov 2025), EvoMaster (Apr 2026) and WMLLM (2026) use the n = 29 determinant task as a benchmark and do not beat the 2003 record (ThetaEvolve scores 0.5764 against a best known of 320/342 ≈ 0.936 under its own normalisation). The 2026 Williamson–Yacobi–Zinn-Justin transformer paper concerns Hadamard existence at orders already settled. I found no Lean or formal proof of the ±1 bullet, and the Epoch page for 668 lists no Lean proof. Two close calls: whether the 668 announcement counts as a settled case of this bullet (for n ≡ 0 mod 4 it is equivalent to the Hadamard-existence question, which the bullet does not ask, but the value of md(668) is what the bullet asks for); and whether Claude's role is load-bearing (the attribution is team credit; the mechanism is not described). Smaller discrepancies I did not settle: the WMLLM arXiv date (2 Jun 2026 on the page, 2609 identifier), the order range of the transformer paper (100–200 on the page, 100–250 in a search summary), and the 2025 date of the Eliahou paper (received 24 Sep 2025 per a snippet).
competing_reading: The strongest reading against counting anything in the window as settling this bullet: the 668 matrix exists only in secondary reports, with no primary text, technical report, or independent check I could find, and Epoch's label is provisional; so the bullet's value at 668 is unsettled on the record I can verify. The Butbaia et al. records are lower bounds only, with optimality shown only within a family; its v1 had no learning method, and the learning component is credited for three of the listed orders by its own appendix. On that reading the maximal determinant of ±1 matrices is unchanged in general, and the AI-involved events are a claimed construction without a primary account plus a search heuristic that found lower bounds. The opposite reading: a valid Hadamard matrix of order 668 is a settled case in the window (md(668) = 668^334), credited to a team including an AI system by its own organisers' labelling, and the Butbaia et al. preprint is a second in-window event in which AI-driven (RL) search produced records. Both readings rest on the same two events; they differ in whether an unverified or lower-bound-only result is counted.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The primary announcement for the order-668 matrix (the X thread or a technical report from Alpöge, Voinov and Reynolds-Haertle), including the decoder and the authors' own sentence on what Claude contributed; (2) an independent check that the decoded matrix is ±1 with HH^T = 668I, and the same for the other claimed orders (716, 892, 1132, 1244, 1388, 1436, 1676, 1772, 1916, 1948, 1964); (3) Epoch's page changelog after 16 Sep 2026, and whether its label changes; (4) the Butbaia et al. repository's verify.py output and a rerun of the determinant ratios at n = 51 and 103–119, the published version of the paper and any referee reports, and the author-side account of which method produced each record (the Appendix A.1 and D statements); (5) the v1 and v3 texts directly, to confirm the scope change and whether the RL policy is load-bearing at 103, 111 and 115; (6) any later paper citing 2608.22518 or the 668 announcement (the 2609.18380 PDF reference list was unreadable to me); (7) the current Orrick maxdet table or the Brent maxdet pages, to check the stated 2012 benchmark values for 103–119.

event.what_happened: On 12 Aug 2026 Levent Alpöge (described by QbitAI and Epoch as an Anthropic researcher) posted on X a ±1 matrix of order 668 with HH^T = 668I, encoded in the post and its replies as a puzzle whose decoder is a shell script (per secondary reports). Per QbitAI (13 Aug 2026, Chinese language, quoting the post) the collaborators are Philippe Voinov, Saul Reynolds-Haertle and Claude; QbitAI and Epoch say the same package gives Hadamard matrices for every open order below 2000 without a known instance (QbitAI lists twelve: 668, 716, 892, 1132, 1244, 1388, 1436, 1676, 1772, 1916, 1948, 1964; Epoch says 'all admissible orders up to 2000 where no such instance was previously known'). The X post itself returned HTTP 402 to my fetch, so the primary wording is quoted through a blog post (Nechita) and secondary reports. Epoch's FrontierMath open-problem page lists 'Hadamard Matrix of Order 668' as 'Solved (human + AI)', 'First solved with: Claude (internal Anthropic model)', crediting 'a team of three humans and Claude', with the provisional label dated 12 Aug 2026 in its changelog.
event.revisions: Epoch label 'Solved by AI' provisional from 12 Aug 2026; relabelled 'Solved (human + AI)' on 16 Sep 2026 per Epoch's changelog (as read on the index page).
event.delivers: If the matrix is valid: a Hadamard matrix of order 668 exists, so md(668) = 668^334, Hadamard's bound, attained. That settles n = 668 for this bullet; secondary reports say it settles eleven further multiples of 4 below 2000. It settles nothing for other n, and the general maximal determinant remains open. (For n ≡ 0 mod 4, the maximal determinant equals n^(n/2) exactly when a Hadamard matrix of that order exists, so the existence claim and the bullet's value coincide there.)
event.remains: md(n) for every other n, including n ≡ 1, 2, 3 (mod 4) and all orders outside the claimed list. If any of the eleven secondary-reported orders fails, those cases remain open too.

judgement.why: The statement asks for md(n) for every n, so settling one order (15, 19, 37, 22, 428, 668) is a case and new record determinants are bounds. The order-668 event is a case: for 4 | n a Hadamard matrix attains n^(n/2), so if it is valid it fixes md(668). I marked it checkable because the record describes an explicit matrix that a short HH^T = 668I script would verify. I marked it doubtful because it reaches us only through secondary sources. Its AI role was the close call. The authors' only words are 'of course claude:))'. Epoch credits 'a team of three humans and Claude' as the solvers. Read together, these support Claude producing part of the construction, but they do not show that Claude produced it with humans only checking, so I chose assisted over generated or none. Butbaia et al. raises lower bounds at n = 51 and 103–119, so it is a bound, checkable through its CSV and verify script. By the authors' own appendix, their learning policies produced the records at 103, 111 and 115, so it is assisted. The methods are the authors' own neural RL policies, not a named model. Eliahou's mod-64 matrix and the complex and roots-of-unity papers are variants. The benchmarks, the failed AI attempts and the transformer paper at already-settled orders are none.
judgement.doubts: The 668 AI role depends on a thin quote plus third-party labelling. A technical report could move it to generated, or to none. Whether a custom RL policy (GNN/transformer trained with PPO) counts as an 'AI system' for the project is a definitional question; I treated it as one. The Butbaia quotes come from a summarising fetch. The record does not establish journal acceptance for Orrick 2004 or Brent et al. 2011, so those stay unreviewed. Orrick–Solomon was published in Discrete Math. (2007) per OEIS.
